questions.title: Two Pointer Pattern
questions.direct_answer: Two indices traversing an array (or two arrays) — converging (from both ends toward center), same-direction (fast/slow), or from two starts. O(n) where nested loops would be O(n²).

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[abcba] --> P1[i=0, j=4: a==a]
    P1 --> P2[i=1, j=3: b==b]
    P2 --> P3[i=2, j=2: cross → TRUE]
    B[hello] --> Q1[i=0, j=4: h!=o]
    Q1 --> F[FALSE]
    C[cycle: fast=2x slow] --> M[they meet → cycle exists]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The pattern's correctness argument (why you can skip): for the converging two-sum on sorted data — arr[i] + arr[j] < target means arr[i] can't pair with ANYTHING at or after j (all would be smaller) — so i++ is safe. Each step eliminates a range, not just a pair — that's the O(n) despite the two pointers.

The fast/slow cycle detection (Floyd's tortoise and hare): slow moves 1, fast moves 2 — if there's a cycle, fast laps slow (they meet); if not, fast reaches nil. The subtle part: they meet INSIDE the cycle, not necessarily at the entry — the follow-up (finding the entry point) is the k=distance-from-head-to-entry trick.

The pattern's limits: it requires the ability to ORDER the decisions (sorted, symmetric, or sequential). On unordered data with pair-target questions, the hash map is the correct O(n) — the two-pointer degenerates to O(n²) without the ordering to exploit.
